title: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
summary: Compute edit distances, rank corrections with the noisy channel, compare Jaro-Winkler, trigram, token and phonetic scores, index with trigrams, BK-trees, automata and SymSpell, then build a tuned record linker.
outcomes: Compute a Levenshtein distance by filling the Wagner-Fischer table and tracing back the edits
Explain how OSA, true Damerau-Levenshtein and Indel distance differ, and why fuzz.ratio is Indel based
Rank spelling corrections with the noisy channel, combining weighted edit costs and word frequency
Compute Jaro-Winkler and trigram Jaccard scores and predict which pairs each metric misjudges

lessons.title: Why exact matching fails and what an edit distance counts

blocks.md:
A user types `recieve` into a search box. A recruiter searches for `google` while the profile says `Google LLC`, where LLC (limited liability company) is a legal suffix. A product feed lists `Acme Corp` and another lists `Corp Acme`. Exact equality says none of these match, and even a substring test such as SQL `LIKE '%recieve%'` (the percent signs match any run of characters, so it asks whether recieve appears anywhere in the stored text) finds nothing, because the typo is *inside* the word.

Fuzzy matching replaces the yes or no test with a number: a **distance** (how many changes separate two strings, lower is closer) or a **similarity** (a score, usually from 0 to 1 or 0 to 100, higher is closer). You then match when the number passes a threshold, or rank candidates by it.

The classic distance counts **edits**, where one edit is a single-character change:

- **insertion**: add a character (`sic` to `sick`)
- **deletion**: remove a character (`black` to `lack`)
- **substitution**: replace one character with another (`box` to `fox`)

The **Levenshtein distance** between two strings is the minimum number of these edits needed to turn one into the other. It is named after Vladimir Levenshtein, whose paper appeared in Russian in 1965 and in English in 1966.

blocks.title: Three edits turn kitten into sitting

scenes.caption: Line the two words up column by column. The dash marks a position where kitten has no character. Most columns already agree.
Columns 1 to 3 and 5 agree, so they cost nothing. Column 0 needs a substitution (k to s): 1 edit so far.
Column 4 needs a second substitution (e to i). Two edits so far.
Column 6 inserts g. Total: 3 edits. No shorter sequence exists, so the Levenshtein distance is 3. Lesson 2 shows how to prove that without guessing alignments.

blocks.prompt: What is the Levenshtein distance between `form` and `from`? A person sees one mistake: two letters swapped.
blocks.reveal: **2**, not 1. Levenshtein has no swap operation, so the cheapest fix is two substitutions (o to r, r to o). Swapped adjacent letters are one of the most common typing errors, which is why lesson 3 adds a **transposition** edit.

blocks.md:
Write $d(x,y)$ for the Levenshtein distance between strings $x$ and $y$, and $|x|$ for the length of $x$ (in this course, bars around a string always mean its length). The distance has properties you will rely on later:

- $d(x,x)=0$ and $d(x,y)=d(y,x)$ (symmetric). Every edit can be undone by one edit (an insertion by a deletion, a substitution by substituting back), so the same number of edits works in both directions.
- **Triangle inequality**: $d(x,z) \le d(x,y)+d(y,z)$. Why: editing $x$ into $y$ and then $y$ into $z$ is one valid way to turn $x$ into $z$, and the cheapest way can only be cheaper.

A distance with these properties, which is also 0 only for identical strings, is called a **metric**, and a set of items with a metric is a **metric space**. Anything proved for metric spaces in general then works on strings, which lesson 7 exploits to prune a search.

- **Length bounds**: $|\,|x|-|y|\,| \le d(x,y) \le \max(|x|,|y|)$. In words, the distance is at least the difference of the two lengths and at most the longer length. You need at least one insertion or deletion per character of length difference, and you never need more edits than the longer string has characters.

A raw distance is hard to threshold. Two edits between `lewenstein` and `levenshtein` (11 characters) is a near match; two edits between `ab` and `abcd` changes half the string. So libraries also report a **normalized similarity** that divides by the largest possible distance, which the length bound says is the longer length, $\max(|x|,|y|)$. Subtracting that fraction from 1 turns it around: 1 means identical, 0 means as far apart as two strings of those lengths can be.

blocks.caption: For kitten and sitting: 1 - 3/7 = 0.571. For lewenstein and levenshtein: 1 - 2/11 = 0.818. For ab and abcd: 1 - 2/4 = 0.5.

blocks.md: A distance counts edits (lower is closer). A similarity is a normalized score (higher is closer). The same raw distance means very different things for short and long strings, so either normalize or make the allowed number of edits depend on length.

blocks.question: A search box accepts any dictionary word within 2 Levenshtein edits of the query. For which query is this rule most likely to return junk?
options: `cat` (3 letters)
`restaurant` (10 letters)
`levenshtein` (11 letters)
All three are equally safe because the threshold is the same
blocks.explain: Two edits can rewrite 2 of the 3 letters of `cat`, so `cut`, `bag`, `act` and many other 3-letter words all match. For a 10 or 11 letter word, 2 edits keep most of the string intact. This is why search engines scale the allowed edits with term length (lesson 8).

blocks.question: You know $d(a,b)=1$ and $d(b,c)=2$ under Levenshtein distance. What does the triangle inequality tell you about $d(a,c)$?
options: It is exactly 3
It is at most 3, and at least 1
It is at least 3
Nothing, because edit distance is not a metric
blocks.explain: The triangle inequality gives the upper bound $d(a,c) \le 1+2 = 3$. Applied the other way, $d(b,c) \le d(b,a)+d(a,c)$, so $d(a,c) \ge 2-1 = 1$. These two bounds are exactly what a BK-tree uses in lesson 7 to skip whole subtrees.

lessons.title: Filling the Wagner-Fischer table cell by cell

blocks.md:
Trying every possible sequence of edits is exponential. The fix is **dynamic programming**: solve the problem for every pair of *prefixes*, smallest first, and reuse the answers. Define $D[i][j]$ as the edit distance between the first $i$ characters of $a$ and the first $j$ characters of $b$, and write $a_i$ for the $i$-th character of $a$. The answer is the bottom-right cell $D[|a|][|b|]$.

This algorithm was discovered independently many times; it carries the name of Wagner and Fischer, who published it in 1974 as the string-to-string correction problem.

blocks.tex: D[i][j] = \min\begin{cases} D[i-1][j] + 1 & \text{delete } a_i \\ D[i][j-1] + 1 & \text{insert } b_j \\ D[i-1][j-1] + [a_i \ne b_j] & \text{match or substitute} \end{cases}
blocks.caption: The bracket is 1 when the characters differ and 0 when they match. Base cases: D[i][0] = i (delete all i characters) and D[0][j] = j (insert all j characters).

blocks.md:
In words: $D[i][j]$ is the smallest of three numbers: the cell above plus 1, the cell to the left plus 1, and the diagonal cell plus 0 if $a_i$ equals $b_j$ or plus 1 if not.

Read each cell as: the best way to align these two prefixes must end with one of three moves. Coming **from above** means the last character of $a$ was deleted. Coming **from the left** means the last character of $b$ was inserted. Coming **diagonally** means the two last characters were aligned, for free if they are equal and for 1 if not. Every cell depends only on its upper, left and upper-left neighbours, so you can fill the table row by row.

blocks.prompt: In the table below, cell $D[2][2]$ compares `ki` with `si`. The last characters match (i and i), and $D[1][1]=1$. What value goes in $D[2][2]$?
blocks.reveal: **1**. When the last characters match, the diagonal move costs nothing, so $D[2][2]=D[1][1]+0=1$. The other two moves give $D[1][2]+1=3$ and $D[2][1]+1=3$. The only edit needed so far is the k to s substitution.

blocks.title: Levenshtein table for kitten (rows) vs sitting (columns)

scenes.caption: Base cases first. Row ε (the empty string) is the cost of building each prefix of sitting from nothing (j insertions); column ε is the cost of deleting each prefix of kitten (i deletions).
Row k. Cell (k, s): k differs from s, so take 1 + min(0, 1, 1) = 1. The rest of the row grows by one per column: each extra letter of sitting must be inserted.
Row i. Cell (i, i) matches, so it copies its diagonal neighbour: D[2][2] = D[1][1] = 1. A match never adds cost.
Rows t and t. Both cells on the diagonal match again, so kitt vs sitt still costs only 1 (the k to s substitution).
Row e. Cell (e, i): the letters differ. Diagonal gives 1 + 1 = 2, above gives 2 + 1 = 3, left gives 2 + 1 = 3. The minimum is 2: a second substitution.
Row n. Cell (n, n) matches, so it copies 2 from the diagonal. The last cell (n, g) is cheapest from the left: 2 + 1 = 3, meaning insert g. The distance is 3.
Traceback: follow the moves that produced each minimum back from the corner. The path is diagonal (k to s, then four free matches with e to i in between) and one step left (insert g).

blocks.caption: Each row needs only the previous one, so memory is two rows. Time is proportional to the number of cells, |a| x |b|.

blocks.md:
The cost is $O(|a|\cdot|b|)$ time. For two 10-character names that is 100 cells, which is nothing. Comparing one query against a million names is a million tables, which is why lessons 7 and 8 are about *not* doing that.

When you only care whether $d \le k$, two shortcuts apply. First, $D[i][j] \ge |i-j|$ (lesson 1's length bound, applied to prefixes of lengths $i$ and $j$), so only the band of cells within $k$ of the diagonal can hold a value $\le k$, and you can skip the rest. Second, the minimum of a row never decreases from one row to the next: every cell is built from a cell of the previous row by adding 0 or 1, or from its left neighbour by adding 1, so no cell can fall below the previous row's minimum. So once a whole row exceeds $k$ you can stop early. Libraries such as RapidFuzz (a widely used fuzzy matching library for Python) use a `score_cutoff` argument to pick these faster paths.

Production libraries are faster still because of **bit-parallelism**. Look down any column of the table: neighbouring cells always differ by exactly -1, 0 or +1 (a lemma of Masek and Paterson and of Ukkonen, as Gene Myers states it in a 1999 paper). So a column can be stored as its top value plus its *vertical deltas*, and those fit in two bit vectors: one with a 1 wherever the delta is +1, one wherever it is -1. Myers showed how to compute the next column's vectors from the current ones with a fixed sequence of AND, OR, XOR, shift and add instructions (17 bit operations per character in the paper's search algorithm), so one 64-bit word holds 64 cells of a column.

RapidFuzz's docs say it uses Hyyrö's version of this idea when the shorter string has at most 64 characters after removing a shared prefix and suffix, and a blockwise version beyond that: $O(\lceil N/64 \rceil M)$ instead of $O(NM)$. Treat 64 as the word-size factor, not a measured speedup.

blocks.title: One column as deltas and two bit vectors

scenes.caption: Column 5 of the kitten vs sitting table: the distances from each prefix of kitten (row i = 0 to 6) to sitti. Storing it needs one small integer per cell.
Subtract each cell from the one below it. Every vertical delta is -1, 0 or +1; that holds for every column of every Levenshtein table.
Two bit vectors encode the deltas: a 1 in the +1 row where the delta is +1, a 1 in the -1 row where it is -1, zeros elsewhere. The top value and these bits rebuild the column.
Simplified: the real algorithm never builds the integer column. It updates both bit vectors for a whole column at once with word operations, 64 rows per machine word.

blocks.md: The table gives one number, but several different edit sequences can tie for the minimum. The traceback picks one of them. Do not read a single alignment as *the* explanation of how two strings differ.

blocks.question: A teammate initializes the first row as `prev = [0] * (len(b) + 1)` instead of `list(range(len(b) + 1))`. What does the function now compute?
options: The same Levenshtein distance, because row 0 is overwritten anyway
The cost of matching `a` against the best substring of `b` that ends at its last character, because skipping a prefix of `b` becomes free
Always 0
The longest common subsequence length
blocks.explain: Row 0 says how much it costs to consume a prefix of `b` before `a` starts. Setting it to 0 makes that free, so a match may start anywhere in `b`. Sellers used exactly this change in 1980 to turn the distance algorithm into approximate substring search. It is a useful algorithm, but not Levenshtein distance.

blocks.question: You only accept matches with at most 1 edit. The query has 6 characters and a candidate has 9. How much of the DP table must you fill to reject the candidate?
options: All 7 x 10 cells
Only the diagonal band of width 3
None: the length difference already proves the distance is at least 3
Only the last row
blocks.explain: Every character of length difference needs at least one insertion or deletion, so $d \ge 9-6 = 3 > 1$. A length check is the cheapest filter of all and real implementations apply it before touching the table.

lessons.title: Transpositions and Indel: which edits count changes the answer

blocks.md: Which operations you allow, and what each costs, is a modelling choice. Fred Damerau's 1964 study of spelling errors found that about 80 percent of misspellings can be fixed by a single insertion, deletion, substitution, or **transposition** (swapping two adjacent characters). Plain Levenshtein charges 2 for a transposition, so `form` vs `from` scores like two unrelated typos.

The cheapest way to add swaps to the table is **optimal string alignment (OSA)**: one extra case in the recurrence. If the last two characters of each prefix are each other's swap, you may jump back two rows and two columns for a cost of 1.

blocks.tex: \text{if } a_i = b_{j-1} \text{ and } a_{i-1} = b_j:\quad D[i][j] = \min\big(D[i][j],\; D[i-2][j-2] + 1\big)
blocks.caption: In words: when the last two characters of a are the last two of b swapped, the cell may also take the value two rows up and two columns left, plus 1 for the swap. Applied after the three usual moves, for i, j at least 2.

blocks.title: form (rows) vs from (columns): Levenshtein, then OSA

scenes.caption: Plain Levenshtein. Cell (r, o) compares for with fro and holds 2: two substitutions. The final distance is 2.
OSA. At cell (r, o), the last two letters are o r in form and r o in from: a swap. The new case takes D[1][1] + 1 = 0 + 1 = 1.
The cheaper cell flows to the corner: (m, m) matches and copies the diagonal, so the OSA distance is 1.

blocks.md:
OSA has a catch: it never edits the same substring twice. **True (unrestricted) Damerau-Levenshtein** distance is the minimum number of insertions, deletions, substitutions and adjacent transpositions with no such restriction. RapidFuzz's docs show the difference: `OSA.distance("CA", "ABC")` is 3, but `DamerauLevenshtein.distance("CA", "ABC")` is 2. True Damerau-Levenshtein swaps CA to AC and then inserts B between the swapped letters; OSA is not allowed to touch that pair again.

This also means OSA is **not a metric**: $d(\text{CA},\text{AC})=1$ and $d(\text{AC},\text{ABC})=1$, yet $d(\text{CA},\text{ABC})=3 > 1+1$. Lucene (the Apache search library that Elasticsearch is built on) documents the measure of its `FuzzyQuery`, the query for terms within a few edits, as "Damerau-Levenshtein (optimal string alignment)", so in practice the name often means OSA.

Going the other way, the **Indel distance** (short for insertion and deletion) allows only insertions and deletions, each costing 1. A substitution then costs 2 (delete plus insert). The opposite extreme, **Hamming distance**, allows only substitutions, so it is defined only for strings of equal length (codes, fixed-width IDs).

Indel has a neat closed form. A **common subsequence** is a sequence of characters that appear in both strings in the same order, not necessarily next to each other. The characters Indel leaves untouched form a common subsequence, and every other character is deleted from $a$ or inserted from $b$, so the distance is $|a| + |b| - 2 \times$ the length of a longest common subsequence. For `kitten` and `sitting` the longest common subsequence is `ittn` (4 letters), so Indel is 6 + 7 - 8 = 5.

RapidFuzz describes Indel as Levenshtein with weights (1, 1, 2): insertion 1, deletion 1, substitution 2. The Jurafsky and Martin textbook (Speech and Language Processing) uses the same substitution-costs-2 convention. RapidFuzz's popular `fuzz.ratio` is a normalized Indel similarity. It divides by $|a|+|b|$, the largest possible Indel distance (delete all of $a$, then insert all of $b$), subtracts from 1 and scales to 0 to 100:

blocks.caption: Docs example: 'this is a test' vs 'this is a test!' needs 1 insertion over 14 + 15 = 29 characters, so 100 x 28/29 = 96.55. kitten vs sitting: Indel 5, ratio 100 x (1 - 5/13) = 61.54.

blocks.title: Four distances on the same pairs

scenes.caption: kitten vs sitting: two substitutions and an insertion. Indel pays 2 per substitution, so it reports 5.
form vs from: a single swap. Only the transposition-aware measures call it 1 edit.
recieve vs receive, the classic typo: also a swap (ie vs ei), so OSA and Damerau-Levenshtein say 1 while Levenshtein says 2.
CA vs ABC: OSA cannot insert between swapped letters, so it reports 3 while true Damerau-Levenshtein reports 2.

blocks.md: Two libraries that both say "Damerau-Levenshtein" can disagree, and "ratio" in RapidFuzz is Indel based, not Levenshtein based. When a threshold copied from one tool behaves oddly in another, check which distance and which normalization each uses.

blocks.question: What is `fuzz.ratio("test", "tent")` in RapidFuzz?
options: 87.5, because one substitution over 8 characters
50.0, because two of the four letters differ
75.0, because the substitution costs 2 Indel edits over 8 characters
25.0, because only one letter is wrong
blocks.explain: Indel has no substitution, so s to n is a deletion plus an insertion: 2 edits. The lengths sum to 8, so ratio = 100 x (1 - 2/8) = 75. The 87.5 answer assumes a substitution costs 1, which is Levenshtein, not Indel.

blocks.question: You are building a structure whose correctness depends on the triangle inequality (lesson 7). Which distance is unsafe to plug in?
options: Levenshtein
Indel
Optimal string alignment (OSA)
True Damerau-Levenshtein
blocks.explain: OSA violates the triangle inequality: CA to AC is 1, AC to ABC is 1, but CA to ABC is 3. A search structure that prunes with that inequality could skip a real match. Levenshtein, Indel and true Damerau-Levenshtein are metrics.

lessons.title: Weighted edits and the noisy channel: why the likely word wins

blocks.md:
A user types `acress`. Six dictionary words are 1 edit away once transpositions count (lesson 3): actress, cress, caress, access, across and acres. Every score so far calls that a six-way tie. A person would not: across is a common word, and dropping the t from actress is an easy slip, while typing r for c is not.

This lesson turns those two intuitions into one score. The example is the textbook one, from the spelling-correction appendix of Jurafsky and Martin's *Speech and Language Processing*, built on Kernighan, Church and Gale (1990).

The **noisy channel** view treats the typo $x$ as a correct word $w$ that passed through a channel that sometimes garbles letters. Correcting means guessing $w$: the dictionary word with the highest probability given what was typed, $P(w \mid x)$. Bayes' rule rewrites that as $P(x \mid w)P(w)/P(x)$. The denominator $P(x)$ is the same for every candidate, so it can be dropped when we only compare candidates:

blocks.caption: C is the candidate set (here every word within 1 edit). P(w), the prior or language model, says how common the word is. P(x|w), the channel or error model, says how likely this particular slip is when the writer meant w.

blocks.md:
**The prior** comes from counting words in a large corpus. The textbook uses the 404,253,213 words of COCA (the Corpus of Contemporary American English): actress occurs 9,321 times, so $P(\text{actress}) = 9321/404253213 = 0.0000231$.

**The channel** needs data on how people actually mistype. Kernighan, Church and Gale used four **confusion matrices**, tables of counts with one cell per pair of letters: sub[x, y] counts letter x typed as y, del and ins count deletions and insertions given the previous letter, and trans counts swapped letter pairs. A count divided by how often its context occurs gives the probability of that edit: for a substitution, how often the intended letter was typed as the wrong one, divided by how often the intended letter occurs.

blocks.title: acress: prior, channel and their product

scenes.caption: Prior alone, per million words (COCA counts). With a uniform channel, where every slip is equally likely, this is the whole ranking: across, access, acres, actress.
Channel alone, per million: dropping t after c (actress) is the likeliest slip; typing r for c (access) the least likely. acres arises from two different insertions; the bar shows es|e.
Product, times 10^9: across 2.78, actress 2.70, acres 1.02, access 0.019, caress 0.0028, cress 0.00078. access falls from 2nd to 4th; actress climbs from 4th to 2nd.

blocks.md: The model picks across, narrowly, and it is wrong: the sentence was *...a stellar and versatile acress whose combination of sass and glamour...*. A single-word prior cannot see that. With bigram probabilities from COCA (the chance of a word given the word just before it), the textbook gets $P(\text{versatile actress whose}) = 0.000021 \times 0.0010 = 210 \times 10^{-10}$ against about $1 \times 10^{-10}$ for across, and the noisy channel now picks actress. The structure stays the same; only $P(w)$ gets smarter.

blocks.prompt: Peter Norvig's well-known toy corrector has no confusion matrix: every known word 1 edit away beats every known word 2 edits away, and within a distance the most frequent word wins. On Norvig's development set of 270 misspellings, how much accuracy is the frequency tie-break worth?
blocks.reveal: **About 7 points.** We ran Norvig's code with the corpus `big.txt` from the same page: 74.8% correct on the development set (Norvig reports 75%) and 67.5% on the 400-word test set (68% reported). Breaking ties alphabetically instead of by frequency drops that to 67.8% and 62.75% in our run. Ranking by $P(w)$ is not a cosmetic tie-breaker; it is half of the model.

blocks.md:
Norvig's channel is the crudest possible: $P(x \mid w)$ depends only on the number of edits. A softer version, $P(x \mid w)=\alpha^d$ for $d$ edits, lets a common word 2 edits away beat a rare word 1 edit away when it is more than $1/\alpha$ times as frequent. In our run on the same sets (a typed word that is itself in the dictionary competes at $d=0$): $\alpha=0.1$ drops development accuracy to 66.3%, $\alpha=0.01$ gives 73.0%, and anything from $0.001$ down reproduces 74.8%. Small implementation choices move these by a word or two.

A flat price per edit cannot fix Norvig's own example `adres`, which should be `address` (two common doublings, d to dd and s to ss) rather than `acres` (one rare d for c slip). With a cheap edit, the most frequent word 2 edits away is `are`, so that wins instead. The channel has to know *which* edits are cheap.

blocks.caption: Lesson 2's recurrence with every +1 replaced by the cost of that particular edit, and sub(c, c) = 0. If edits are assumed independent and each cost is -log P(edit), the cheapest path is the most probable sequence of edits.

blocks.md: Without an error corpus, keyboard geometry is a cheap stand-in for the confusion matrix: a finger that slips usually hits a neighbouring key. Below, a substitution between adjacent QWERTY keys costs 0.5 and every other edit costs 1 (a simplified layout: three letter rows, each lower row half a key to the right). PostgreSQL's `levenshtein(source, target, ins_cost, del_cost, sub_cost)` and RapidFuzz's `weights=(insertion, deletion, substitution)` accept one cost per operation type; costs that depend on the letters need a loop like this one.

blocks.caption: Output as run. Plain Levenshtein puts word and ward level at 1 edit; the keyboard model prefers word because p sits next to o.

blocks.title: Keyboard-weighted table for wprd (rows) vs word (columns)

scenes.caption: Base cases and row w are the same as in lesson 2: inserting or deleting still costs 1 per character, and w matches w for free.
Cell (p, o): p and o are neighbours on the keyboard, so the diagonal move costs 0.5 instead of 1: D = 0 + 0.5.
r and d then match for free, so the corner holds 0.5. Against ward, p and a are far apart, the same cell costs a full 1 and the distance is 1.0.

blocks.md: This is the score the tie-breakers in later lessons approximate. SymSpell's `Top` and `Closest` settings return the suggestions of the smallest edit distance found, ordered by term frequency, and Elasticsearch's term suggester sorts by similarity score, then document frequency. Both treat edit distance as a coarse channel model and frequency as $P(w)$.

Rank corrections by P(x|w) x P(w): how likely this slip is, times how common the word is. Plain edit distance with a frequency tie-break is the special case where every slip of the same size is equally likely.

A plain noisy channel overcorrects: it replaces correct but rare words, such as names, with frequent ones. Jurafsky and Martin describe how real systems guard against it: never touch some tokens (numbers, single letters), and only correct when the best candidate beats keeping the word by a margin, $\log P(w \mid x) - \log P(x \mid x) > \theta$.

blocks.question: Two candidates are each 1 edit from a typo. Candidate A is 50 times as frequent as B, but B's slip is 100 times as likely as A's according to the confusion matrices. Which one does the noisy channel pick?
options: A, because at equal edit distance the more frequent word always wins
Neither: equal edit distance means a tie that needs a random choice
A, because the prior always outweighs the channel
B, because its product P(x|w) x P(w) is twice A's
blocks.explain: Write A's slip probability as p. A scores p x 50f and B scores 100p x f, so B wins by a factor of 2. Frequency only decides alone when every slip is equally likely, which is the assumption a plain edit distance makes.

blocks.question: Under the noisy channel, when can a candidate 2 edits away beat one that is 1 edit away?
options: When both of its edits are common slips and the word is common enough that its product P(x|w) x P(w) is larger
Never: two edits always multiply to a smaller probability than one
Only when transpositions are switched off
Only when the 1-edit word is missing from the dictionary
blocks.explain: Two likely edits (such as d to dd and s to ss in adres for address) can multiply to more than one unlikely edit (d to c for acres), and the prior can widen the gap. Norvig's corrector forbids this by always preferring distance 1, which is one reason it returns acres.

lessons.title: Jaro-Winkler, trigrams and token scorers on the same pairs

blocks.md: Edit distances treat every position alike and care about word order. Real data breaks both assumptions. People rarely mistype the first letters of a name, and `Corp Acme` is the same company as `Acme Corp` even though Levenshtein needs 8 edits. Three other families of scores handle these cases: **Jaro-Winkler** for short names, **character n-grams** (overlapping runs of n consecutive characters) for order-tolerant matching, and **token-based** scorers for multi-word strings.

**Jaro similarity** comes from **record linkage** (deciding which records in different files describe the same person when there is no shared ID), where it was used to match names across census files. For two strings $s_1$ and $s_2$, two characters *match* if they are equal and no further apart than $\lfloor \max(|s_1|,|s_2|)/2 \rfloor - 1$ positions: a window that grows with the longer length, so a letter only counts if it sits in roughly the same place in both strings. Let $m$ be the number of matches. Walk the matched characters of each string in order; each position where they differ is half a **transposition**, and $t$ is the number of such positions divided by 2, because one swapped pair (th in martha, ht in marhta) shows up as two mismatched positions. William Winkler's 1990 paper then boosts the score when the strings share a prefix, because agreement at the start is strong evidence for names.

blocks.caption: J = 0 when m = 0. Here l is the common prefix length, capped at 4, and p = 0.1 is the prefix scale from Winkler (1990).

blocks.md:
In words: $J$ averages three fractions: the share of $s_1$'s characters that found a match, the same share for $s_2$, and the share of matches that are in the same order, $(m-t)/m$. For identical strings all three are 1, so $J = 1$.

Jaro-Winkler then closes part of the remaining gap $1-J$: a shared prefix of $\ell$ characters closes the fraction $\ell \times p$ of it. That is why $p$ may be at most 0.25: with the prefix capped at 4, 4 x 0.25 = 1 already closes the whole gap, and a larger $p$ would push the score past 1.

blocks.title: Jaro-Winkler for martha vs marhta

scenes.caption: Both strings have 6 characters, so the match window is floor(6/2) - 1 = 2: a character may match one up to 2 positions away.
All 6 characters find a partner within the window (t at 3 matches t at 4, h at 4 matches h at 3). So m = 6.
Matched characters in order: m a r t h a vs m a r h t a. Two positions disagree, so t = 2/2 = 1. J = (6/6 + 6/6 + 5/6)/3 = 0.9444.
Common prefix mar has length 3, so JW = 0.9444 + 3 x 0.1 x (1 - 0.9444) = 0.9611. The shared start pushes the score up.

blocks.md: Implementations differ in details Winkler's paper leaves open. RapidFuzz's `JaroWinkler` uses `prefix_weight=0.1` by default (allowed 0 to 0.25), caps the prefix at 4, and in its source only applies the boost when the Jaro score is above 0.7.

**Trigram similarity** (PostgreSQL's `pg_trgm` extension; trgm is short for trigram) breaks each string into three-character pieces. It lowercases, ignores non-alphanumeric characters, and pads each word with two spaces in front and one behind, so `cat` becomes `"  c"`, `" ca"`, `"cat"`, `"at "`. The similarity is the **Jaccard index** of the two trigram sets: shared trigrams divided by distinct trigrams in either. Because sets ignore order, `Acme Corp` and `Corp Acme` have identical trigram sets and score 1.0. The `%` operator matches when similarity exceeds `pg_trgm.similarity_threshold`, which defaults to 0.3.

blocks.caption: pg_trgm docs example: word vs words share 4 of 7 distinct trigrams, similarity 0.571429.

blocks.md: **Token scorers** in RapidFuzz work on words. `token_sort_ratio` sorts the words of each string and then runs `ratio`. `token_set_ratio` builds three strings: the sorted shared words, the shared words plus the first string's leftover words, and the shared words plus the second string's leftovers. It runs `ratio` on each pair and keeps the highest, so it returns 100 when one string's word set is a subset of the other's (the shared words then are that whole string). `partial_ratio` slides the shorter string along the longer one and keeps the best `ratio`. None of the scorers lowercase by default (`processor=None`): `ratio("Google LLC", "google")` is 62.5, and 75.0 after `utils.default_process`, which lowercases, strips non-alphanumerics and trims.

blocks.prompt: Before you step through the chart: for `Acme Corp` vs `Corp Acme`, which of the six scores will be lowest?
blocks.reveal: **Normalized Levenshtein, at 11.1.** Character by character the strings line up badly, so it needs 8 edits over 9 characters. Trigram Jaccard, `token_sort_ratio` and `token_set_ratio` all give 100 because they ignore word order. No single metric wins every pair; the chart shows each one failing somewhere.

blocks.title: Six scores (0 to 100) on six pairs, after default_process

scenes.caption: recieve vs receive. Jaro-Winkler likes the long shared prefix (96.7). Trigram Jaccard is only 33.3: the swap destroys every trigram in the middle of the word.
Google LLC vs google. token_set_ratio gives 100 because {google} is a subset of {google, llc}. Character metrics charge for the missing suffix.
Acme Corp vs Corp Acme. Order-blind scores (trigrams, token sort, token set) give 100; Levenshtein gives 11.1.
Dwayne vs Duane, a name pair from Winkler's paper. Jaro-Winkler 84.0 is the most forgiving; trigrams give 18.2 because short words have few trigrams.
Austria vs Australia: different countries, yet Jaro-Winkler gives 92.7 and fuzz.ratio 87.5. High similarity is not the same as the same entity.
New York Mets vs New York Yankees: different teams. token_set_ratio still gives 76.2 from the shared words new york. Thresholds must be tuned on labelled pairs from your data, as lesson 9 does.

blocks.md: `partial_ratio` produces false positives on short strings: `fuzz.partial_ratio("ai", "said hello")` is 100 because `ai` appears inside `said`. Likewise `token_set_ratio` returns 100 for any subset, so `google` vs `google cloud platform team` is a perfect score. Use these scorers with a minimum length or combine them with other evidence.

Every score here counts Unicode code points, not visible characters. `café` can store é as one code point (NFC) or as e plus a combining accent (NFD). The two look identical, yet their Levenshtein distance is 2, while each is 1 edit from `cafe`. Normalize before scoring: NFKC, then casefold, then strip accents if your data allows. The cleaning lesson of the entity-normalization course covers this.

blocks.question: Using the Jaro-Winkler formula with p = 0.1: `dwayne` vs `duane` has Jaro similarity 0.8222 and shares only the first letter. What is the Jaro-Winkler score?
options: 0.8222, because a prefix of 1 earns no boost
blocks.explain: JW = J + l x p x (1 - J) = 0.8222 + 1 x 0.1 x 0.1778 = 0.8400. Every shared leading character (up to 4) moves the score a tenth of the remaining distance toward 1.

blocks.question: You match company names where one source often adds suffixes such as LLC or Inc and words are sometimes reordered. Which scorer handles both cases, and what must you watch for?
options: fuzz.ratio; it is the most precise
Jaro-Winkler; it rewards shared prefixes
partial_ratio; it finds the best substring
token_set_ratio; it ignores order and extra words, but any subset scores 100, so very short names can match too much
blocks.explain: token_set_ratio ignores word order and scores 100 when one word set contains the other, which absorbs added suffixes. The same property means a one-word name like `google` scores 100 against any longer name containing it, so pair it with a length check or a second score.

lessons.title: Phonetic keys: Soundex, Metaphone and Daitch-Mokotoff

blocks.md:
Smith and Smyth differ by one letter, but Catherine and Kathryn are 4 Levenshtein edits apart and Philips and Fillips 3, although each pair sounds the same. Clerks writing down names they heard, and people spelling names from memory, make errors of sound rather than of typing.

A **phonetic key** replaces a name with a short code meant to capture its pronunciation. Names that sound alike should get the same code, which can then be compared, indexed or grouped by plain equality.

**Soundex** is the oldest: Robert C. Russell patented it in 1918 and 1922, and it was used to index US census records. The National Archives' rules: keep the first letter, give the other consonants a digit by sound group, ignore a, e, i, o, u, h, w and y, code adjacent letters with the same digit (including the first letter) once, but code a digit again when a vowel separates the two letters (h and w do not separate), and pad with zeros or cut to one letter plus three digits. The digit groups:

- 1: b, f, p, v
- 2: c, g, j, k, q, s, x, z
- 3: d, t
- 4: l
- 5: m, n
- 6: r

blocks.title: Soundex by the National Archives rules

scenes.caption: Robert: keep R, and remember its digit 6 so that a second r right after it would not be coded again.
o is a vowel: no digit, and last is reset, so a repeated digit after a vowel is coded again. Then b gives 1.
e resets last; r gives 6; t gives 3. Four characters are enough.
Rupert walks the same path (u, p=1, e, r=6, t=3), so both names get R163 although they are different names.
Ashcraft: s gives 2. Then h is skipped without resetting last, so it does not separate s from the next letter.
c also has digit 2 and last is still 2, so it is not coded. r, f and t follow; the result is cut to four characters.
scenes.output:
Robert R163
Rupert R163
Ashcraft A261

blocks.md: That h and w rule is where implementations part ways. The National Archives page says Ashcraft is coded A-261, "not A-226". PostgreSQL 17's `soundex('Ashcraft')` returns `A226` (we ran it), while the Python library jellyfish returns A261. On the 1,000 most common surnames of the 1990 US census list the two agree on every name, so the difference bites only on names like Ashcraft, but codes from two systems are only comparable if both use the same variant.

**Metaphone** (Lawrence Philips, 1990) replaces the fixed letter table with rules about English spelling, for example *drop the first letter of KN, GN, PN, AE, WR* and *drop B after M at the end of a word*. GNU aspell uses Metaphone codes to find suggestions whose pronunciation is a short edit distance from the typo.

**Double Metaphone** returns two codes, a primary and an alternate, because many names, especially non-English ones, can be pronounced two ways. PostgreSQL's `dmetaphone('Schwarz')` gives XRS and `dmetaphone_alt('Schwarz')` gives XFRT. Below we count a match when any code of one name equals any code of the other.

**Daitch-Mokotoff Soundex** was designed to work far better for non-English names. Per the PostgreSQL docs, it codes the first six meaningful letters instead of four, maps letters and letter combinations to ten possible codes instead of seven, codes two letters with a single sound as one number, and emits several codes when a spelling has several plausible sounds. `daitch_mokotoff('John')` returns {160000, 460000}; Schwarz gives {479400, 474000} and Shwartz {479400}, so the two overlap. The docs suggest treating any overlap as a match.

blocks.prompt: Robert and Rupert are different given names. Will Soundex, Double Metaphone and Daitch-Mokotoff keep them apart?
blocks.reveal: **No, all three merge them**: Soundex R163, Double Metaphone RPRT, Daitch-Mokotoff 979300 (PostgreSQL output). By contrast Levenshtein says 2 edits and Jaro-Winkler 0.80, which a 0.85 threshold would reject. A phonetic key is coarse by design: it trades precision for recall.

blocks.title: Eight name pairs: edit scores vs phonetic keys

scenes.caption: Columns: normalized Levenshtein similarity, Jaro-Winkler, then 1 if the Soundex codes are equal, if any Double Metaphone codes agree, if the Daitch-Mokotoff code sets overlap (PostgreSQL 17 output).
Phonetic keys catch sound-alikes that edit scores rate low: Philips/Fillips is only 0.57 by Levenshtein. Soundex still misses both because it keeps the first letter as written (C vs K, P vs F).
Keys disagree with each other: only Daitch-Mokotoff links Schwarz/Shwartz, and Knight/Night (silent k) needs Double Metaphone, which codes the first sound.
Over-merging: every key links Robert/Rupert and Lee/Liu, different names. Jaro-Winkler 0.80 and 0.56 would keep them apart at 0.85.

blocks.md: How coarse are the codes? On the 1,000 most common surnames of the [1990 US census list](https://www2.census.gov/topics/genealogy/1990surnames/dist.all.last), PostgreSQL's Soundex produces only 618 distinct codes: 600 of the names share a code with at least one other, 782 pairs collide, and the largest group has 14 names (Reese, Reyes, Rice, Rich, Riggs, Rios, Roach, Rocha, Rosa, Rose, Ross, Ruiz, Rush, Russo: all R200). Double Metaphone's primary code gives 650 codes and 677 colliding pairs; Daitch-Mokotoff, with several codes per name, makes 1,155 overlapping pairs. Only 236 pairs on the same list are within 1 Levenshtein edit.

blocks.title: Matching pairs among 1,000 common US surnames

scenes.caption: Pairs of different surnames that each method calls a match (1990 census top 1,000, computed with PostgreSQL 17 and RapidFuzz). As a blocking key that is fine: a block of 14 is cheap to compare.
As a final decision it is not: most of these pairs are simply different surnames. A phonetic code is evidence that two names might match, not proof.

blocks.md: PostgreSQL ships all of these in the `fuzzystrmatch` extension: `soundex`, `difference` (how many of the four Soundex characters agree, 0 to 4), `metaphone`, `dmetaphone`, `dmetaphone_alt` and `daitch_mokotoff`, next to `levenshtein`. The docs carry two cautions: Soundex is not very useful for non-English names, and `soundex`, `metaphone`, `dmetaphone` and `dmetaphone_alt` do not work well with multibyte encodings such as UTF-8, so use `daitch_mokotoff` or `levenshtein` for such data.

blocks.caption: Outputs as returned by PostgreSQL 17. The && operator tests whether two arrays share an element.

blocks.md: In Elasticsearch, the phonetic analysis plugin adds a `phonetic` token filter. Its `encoder` accepts metaphone (the default), double_metaphone, soundex, refined_soundex, caverphone1, caverphone2, cologne, nysiis, koelnerphonetik, haasephonetik, beider_morse and daitch_mokotoff. With `replace: false` the original and phonetic tokens are stacked at the same position, and the docs warn that the fuzzy match query does not apply fuzziness to stacked tokens. They recommend separate fields with and without phonetic filtering, queried together with different boosts.

Use a phonetic code as a blocking key or as one comparison level that adds some evidence, never as the final decision. It merges different names, its rules are tied to one language's spelling, and implementations disagree. The entity-normalization course shows how such levels feed a match weight.

Soundex keeps the first letter as written, so names that differ only in their first letter never match: Caitlin and Kaitlyn get C345 and K345, Philips and Fillips P412 and F412. If you block on Soundex, add a second key that does not depend on the first letter.

blocks.question: Which pair does Soundex merge that a Jaro-Winkler threshold of 0.85 keeps apart, and what does that mean if you match on Soundex alone?
options: Smith and Smyth; matching on Soundex alone raises precision
Caitlin and Kaitlyn; matching on Soundex alone lowers recall
Robert and Rupert (Jaro-Winkler 0.80); matching on Soundex alone adds false matches and lowers precision
Schwarz and Shwartz; nothing changes because both methods agree
blocks.explain: Robert and Rupert share R163 but score 0.80 by Jaro-Winkler. Smith/Smyth is matched by both, Caitlin/Kaitlyn is matched by neither (C345 vs K345, 0.81), and Schwarz/Shwartz gets different Soundex codes (S620, S632). Codes that merge different names create false matches, which costs precision.

blocks.question: You store 50 million customer surnames in PostgreSQL as UTF-8, many of them non-English, and want a fast sounds-like lookup. Which choice fits the docs?
options: soundex(), because it is the census standard
daitch_mokotoff() with a GIN index and the && overlap operator
dmetaphone(), because it has no input length limit
difference(surname, query) > 2 evaluated on every row
blocks.explain: The docs say soundex, metaphone and dmetaphone do not work well with multibyte encodings such as UTF-8 and that Soundex is weak for non-English names. daitch_mokotoff handles both, returns an array that a GIN index can serve, and && finds any shared code. difference() on every row is a full scan.

lessons.title: Indexes that skip most strings: trigram filters and BK-trees

blocks.md:
Everything so far compares one pair. A real lookup compares one query against a whole column or dictionary, and running the DP table against a million names per keystroke is too slow. Indexes avoid it in two ways:

1. **Filter then verify**: a cheap index proposes a small set of candidates that *might* be close, then the exact score runs only on those.
2. **Prune with the triangle inequality**: organize strings by their distances to each other so whole groups can be ruled out without comparing against them.

The filter idea rests on the **q-gram lemma**. A **q-gram** is a run of $q$ consecutive characters (the same idea as an n-gram, with the length called $q$). One edit can destroy at most $q$ of a string's overlapping q-grams: it changes only the windows that cover the edited position, and at most $q$ windows of length $q$ cover any one position. A string of length $m$ has $m-q+1$ q-grams (a window can start at positions 1 to $m-q+1$), so any string within $k$ edits of it still shares at least $m-q+1-kq$ of them. For `recieve` ($m=7$, $q=3$, $k=1$) that is $5-3=2$ unpadded trigrams; `relieve`, one edit away, shares exactly two (`iev`, `eve`). A string that shares fewer than the bound cannot be within $k$ edits and is skipped without computing a distance.

PostgreSQL builds this with a **GIN** index (generalized inverted index, `gin_trgm_ops`), an inverted index from each trigram to the rows containing it, or a **GiST** index (generalized search tree, `gist_trgm_ops`), which stores each row's trigram set as a bitmap signature: a fixed-length bit string in which each trigram sets one bit, compact but lossy. The list of rows stored under one trigram is its **posting list**. A query extracts its own trigrams, reads only the matching posting lists, and rechecks similarity on the candidates. Below, the query `recieve` has 8 padded trigrams; the chart shows ten dictionary words.

blocks.title: Step 1: shared trigrams read from the posting lists

scenes.caption: Each of the 8 query trigrams has a posting list; counting hits per word gives these overlaps. banana shares none and is never touched. In a large dictionary most rows share nothing with the query.

blocks.title: Steps 2 and 3: score and rank the candidates

scenes.caption: Step 2: compute the Jaccard similarity (x100) for the nine candidates only. Four words reach the default threshold of 30: relieve 45.5, retrieve 41.7, recipe 36.4, receive 33.3.

Step 3: rank. The intended word receive comes last of the four, because the ie swap breaks the middle trigrams. Rerank with an edit distance: OSA puts receive and relieve level at 1 edit, ahead of retrieve and recipe at 2.

blocks.md: Do not confuse the count filter with pg_trgm's `%` operator. The q-gram lemma guarantees that a string within $k$ edits shares at least a certain number of grams. The `%` operator instead thresholds the Jaccard *similarity*, which carries no edit-distance guarantee: PostgreSQL returns `similarity('cat', 'cut')` = 0.143, far below the default 0.3, although the words are 1 edit apart. Short words have few trigrams and one edit breaks most of them (for `cat` the lemma's bound is $3-3+1-3=-2$, so it cannot filter anything either). Even `receive` passes for `recieve` only narrowly, at 0.333. When you need every word within $k$ edits, use an edit-distance structure; use `%` as a recall-oriented filter and rerank.

blocks.caption: Patterns from the pg_trgm documentation. The same trigram indexes also accelerate LIKE, ILIKE and regular-expression searches.

blocks.md: The second idea is the **BK-tree** of Burkhard and Keller (1973), probably the first general structure for searching a metric space. Pick any string as the root. Every other string goes into the child subtree labelled by its distance to the root, and the same rule applies recursively. To find everything within radius $r$ of query $q$: compute $d = d(q, \text{node})$, report the node if $d \le r$, and descend only into children whose label $i$ satisfies $d-r \le i \le d+r$. The triangle inequality guarantees that every skipped subtree holds only strings farther than $r$. Why: a string $u$ in the child labelled $i$ is exactly $i$ from the node. If $u$ were within $r$ of $q$, then $i \le d + r$ (go from the node to $q$, then to $u$) and $d \le r + i$ (go from $q$ to $u$, then to the node), which is exactly the range above.

blocks.title: BK-tree search for cape within 1 edit

scenes.caption: Ten words inserted in the order book, books, cake, boo, boon, cook, cape, cart, bolt, look. Each edge label is the Levenshtein distance from child to parent.
Compare cape with the root: d(cape, book) = 4. With r = 1 only children labelled 3 to 5 can hold a match, so only the edge labelled 4 is followed.
Six words are ruled out without computing their distance. Next, d(cape, cake) = 1, which is within the radius: cake is a result. Children labelled 0 to 2 may hold matches, so both are visited.
d(cape, cape) = 0 is a match; d(cape, cart) = 2 is not. Result: cake and cape, found with 4 distance computations instead of 10.

blocks.prompt: Same tree, query `bool` with radius 1. Its distance to the root `book` is 1. How many of the ten words must be compared?
blocks.reveal: **7.** With $d=1$ and $r=1$, children labelled 0 to 2 qualify, so `books` (1) and `bolt` (2) are followed and only the `cake` subtree (3 words) is skipped. Results: book, boo and boon. Pruning works best when the query is far from a node relative to $r$; a query close to the root prunes little.

blocks.md: Both indexes trade exactness of the first step for speed: a trigram index proposes candidates by a cheap overlap count, a BK-tree rules out subtrees with the triangle inequality. Neither changes the final score; you still verify candidates with the metric you trust.

blocks.question: In a BK-tree, the query is at distance 3 from a node and the search radius is 1. Which child subtrees are searched?
options: Only the child labelled 3
Children labelled 2, 3 and 4
Children labelled 0 to 4
All children, because 3 > 1
blocks.explain: Any match $u$ in a child labelled $i$ has $d(u,\text{node}) = i$ and $d(q,u) \le 1$, so by the triangle inequality $|i-3| \le 1$, giving $i \in \{2,3,4\}$. Every other child provably contains no match.

blocks.question: A trigram index returns `receive` as a candidate for `recieve`, but ranks it below `relieve`. What is the best fix?
options: Lower the similarity threshold to 0.1
Rerank the candidates the index returns with an edit distance that counts transpositions
Switch to a GiST index
Use 4-grams instead of trigrams
blocks.explain: The index did its job: receive is in the candidate set. Its ordering reflects trigram overlap, which a swap in the middle of a word damages. Reranking with OSA or Damerau-Levenshtein lifts receive (1 edit) into a tie with relieve (also 1 edit, a substitution), ahead of retrieve and recipe (2 edits); word frequency (lesson 4's P(w)) then decides. Lowering the threshold only adds candidates, and longer grams are damaged even more by a swap.

lessons.title: Levenshtein automata, SymSpell and fuzzy queries in production

blocks.md: Search engines face the dictionary version of the problem: find every indexed *term* within $k$ edits of a query term. Before Lucene 4.0, `FuzzyQuery` did the obvious thing: visit every unique term in the index, compute its edit distance, and keep the close ones. Lucene 4.0 replaced that with a **Levenshtein automaton**: a deterministic finite automaton (DFA), a machine that reads a string one character at a time, moves between a fixed set of states, and accepts or rejects it at the end. This one accepts exactly the strings within $k$ edits of the query term, built with the construction of Schulz and Mihov ([Fast string correction with Levenshtein automata](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10032-002-0082-8), 2002).

Lucene intersects that automaton with the sorted term dictionary (the index's alphabetical list of every distinct term), so it seeks and scans only the regions that can still match. Michael McCandless's write-up of the change is titled *Lucene's FuzzyQuery is 100 times faster in 4.0*.

The intuition comes straight from the DP table. Fix the query and read a candidate one character at a time; after each character the current DP row summarizes everything that matters about the prefix read so far. That row is the automaton's **state**. If every entry in the row exceeds $k$, no continuation can bring the distance back down, so every term with this prefix is rejected at once. In a sorted dictionary, all terms sharing a prefix sit next to each other, so the whole block is skipped.

A DFA needs a *finite* set of states, and raw rows are not finite: after reading `jazzyjazzy` against `fuzzy` the row is [10, 10, 10, 9, 8, 7], and longer terms push it higher. The fix: once an entry exceeds $k$ its exact value no longer matters, so cap every entry at $k+1$ (here every entry becomes 2). Capped rows have $|q|+1$ entries, each between 0 and $k+1$, so only finitely many exist. Counting by script the capped rows reachable for `fuzzy`: 20 for $k=1$, 49 for $k=2$, 113 for $k=3$ (each including the dead state).

Schulz and Mihov go one step further: only a window of $2k+1$ query positions around the current position can still matter, so a state can be written relative to that position, and each transition depends only on which of those query characters equal the next input character. Then one table serves every query. Lucene's tables, generated with the Moman package, have 5 such parametric states for 1 edit and 30 for 2 (6 and 45 with transpositions), each paired with an offset; Lucene ships tables only up to `MAXIMUM_SUPPORTED_DISTANCE = 2`.

blocks.title: Reading terms against the query fuzzy with k = 1

scenes.caption: The start state is row 0 of the table: the cost of matching each prefix of fuzzy against nothing.
Read j. The row minimum is 1, which is still within k = 1, so keep reading.
Read a. Every entry is now at least 2, so no term starting with ja can be within 1 edit of fuzzy. Reject after 2 characters, and skip every other ja term too.
Now fuzz. The rows stay on the diagonal: after f, u, z, z the row is [4, 3, 2, 1, 0, 1]. The last entry is 1, so fuzz is accepted (one insertion of y).
scenes.output:
jazzy: rejected after 2 of 5 characters
fuzz: accepted, distance 1

blocks.title: A sorted term dictionary scanned for fuzzy with k = 1

scenes.caption: Brute force (Lucene before 4.0): read every character of every term and finish its full DP table: 58 rows for these 12 terms.
Automaton style: stop each term as soon as its state dies. gauzy and jazzy die after 2 characters; funny, furry and fuss after 4. Matches: fuzz, fuzzy, muzzy.
Simplified: Lucene precomputes the states into DFA tables and seeks through its term dictionary, so blocks of terms behind a dead prefix are skipped without being read at all.

blocks.md: Elasticsearch, the search engine built on Lucene, exposes this machinery in its `fuzzy` query. Its docs describe `fuzziness` as a maximum Levenshtein edit distance, with transpositions counted as one edit by default (`transpositions: true`). The recommended value `AUTO` (equivalent to `AUTO:3,6`, where 3 and 6 are the term lengths at which one edit and then two edits become allowed) scales edits with term length: terms of 0 to 2 characters must match exactly, 3 to 5 allow one edit, and longer terms allow two. `max_expansions` (default 50) caps how many matching terms are used, and `prefix_length` (default 0) requires the first characters to match exactly, which shrinks the search. Lucene's `FuzzyQuery` supports at most 2 edits, and its javadoc warns that higher distances match a large part of the term dictionary.

blocks.caption: recieve has 7 characters, so AUTO allows 2 edits. With transpositions on, receive is only 1 edit away.

blocks.md: **SymSpell** (Wolf Garbe) takes a different route for spelling correction against a fixed dictionary: the *symmetric delete* algorithm. Offline, it generates every string reachable by deleting up to $k$ characters from each dictionary word and stores them in a hash map. At query time it generates the deletes of the query and looks them up.

Deletes alone are enough. An insertion in the query is undone by deleting that character from the query. A deletion in the query is matched by deleting the same character from the dictionary word. A substitution or an adjacent swap is matched by deleting the differing character (or one letter of the swapped pair) from both sides, which leaves the same string. And deletes are few: a 5-letter word has 5 + 10 + 10 = 25 ways to choose 1, 2 or 3 of its positions to delete, so 25 deletes within 3 edits. Candidates are then verified with an actual edit distance computation.

blocks.title: Symmetric delete with k = 1: one-character deletes

scenes.caption: Each row lists the 7 strings made by deleting one character. The dictionary rows were computed in advance and stored in a hash map from delete to word.
Lookup: receve and recive appear in both the query row and the receive row. A shared delete on both sides covers a substitution or, as here, a transposition.

reieve is shared with relieve (substitute c with l). Both candidates are verified with the real distance: receive is 1 (a swap) and relieve is 1 (a substitution). Among the closest, SymSpell prefers the most frequent word: lesson 4's P(w).

blocks.md: The same machinery serves *did you mean*. Elasticsearch's **term suggester** proposes indexed terms within an edit distance of each token of the text and sorts them by similarity score, then document frequency (or frequency first with `sort: frequency`). The **phrase suggester** builds on it: it generates candidates per token the same way and picks whole corrected phrases with an n-gram language model, the context that lesson 4 showed a single-word corrector lacks.

Choose the structure by the job. A search engine field: Elasticsearch or Lucene `fuzzy` with `AUTO`. A database column: `pg_trgm` with a GIN or GiST index, then rerank. Single-word spelling correction against a fixed dictionary: SymSpell or a Levenshtein automaton. Matching names or records: lesson 9 builds that pipeline end to end.

Lucene's javadoc documents a surprise: `FuzzyQuery` on `abcd` with `maxEdits=2` does not match the indexed term `ab`, even though the Levenshtein distance is 2. Engines add rules of their own on top of the textbook distance, so test short terms and other edge cases directly.

blocks.question: With Elasticsearch `fuzziness: AUTO` (default 3,6), how many edits are allowed for the terms `ox`, `cat` and `kitchen`?
options: 2, 2 and 2
1, 1 and 2
0, 1 and 2
0, 1 and 1
blocks.explain: AUTO:3,6 means lengths 0 to 2 must match exactly, 3 to 5 allow one edit, and more than 5 allow two. `ox` has 2 characters (0 edits), `cat` 3 (1 edit), `kitchen` 7 (2 edits).

blocks.question: A Levenshtein automaton for query `fuzzy` with k = 1 reaches a state where every entry of the DP row is 2 after reading `ja`. Why can it reject every term starting with `ja` without reading further?
options: Because terms starting with ja are rare
Because the row minimum never decreases as more characters are read, so the final distance will be at least 2
Because the automaton only accepts terms of exactly 5 characters
Because Lucene sets prefix_length to 2
blocks.explain: Each new cell is at least the minimum of the previous row (diagonal moves add 0 or 1, the others add 1), so a row whose minimum is 2 can only lead to distances of 2 or more. That dead state lets the engine skip the entire ja block of the sorted term dictionary.

blocks.question: SymSpell with k = 1 finds that the query and a dictionary word share a one-character delete, while neither is a delete of the other. What kind of single error explains that?
options: An insertion in the query
A deletion in the query
A substitution or an adjacent transposition
Nothing; it is a false positive that cannot be within 1 edit
blocks.explain: A shared one-character delete fits one differing position (a substitution, like reieve from recieve and relieve) or an adjacent swap (receve from recieve and receive). It does not guarantee 1 edit: abc and bca share the delete bc but are 2 edits apart, so SymSpell verifies every candidate with a real distance.

lessons.title: Build it: match two name lists at scale and pick a threshold

blocks.md: Time to use the toolbox on real-sized data. Two lists describe people, and we must link the records that are the same person. The data is Febrl dataset 4, shipped with the Python recordlinkage package ([dataset docs](https://recordlinkage.readthedocs.io/en/latest/ref-datasets.html)). Febrl (Freely Extensible Biomedical Record Linkage) is the open-source system whose principal developer is Peter Christen; its generator builds records from frequency tables of real names and addresses, then makes duplicates by inserting, deleting or substituting characters and swapping, dropping or merging words. Dataset 4 has 5,000 originals and one corrupted copy of each.

Setup: list A is originals rec-0 to rec-1999; list B is the copies of rec-1500 to rec-3499. So 500 of B's 2,000 records have a true partner in A, hidden among 4,000,000 possible pairs. Each record becomes one key: given name, surname, street name and suburb, joined and cleaned with RapidFuzz's `utils.default_process`. A true pair looks like `niamh tuckwell richman place campbelltown` against `niamh tuckewll richman place campbelltown`; a hard one is `alicia fardell reveley crescent sunshine beach` against `fardwll alicia sunshine jeach`.

The entity-normalization course owns the full linkage pipeline (cleaning rules, blocking measures, match weights, clustering). Here we run the string part end to end: candidates, scores, threshold.

blocks.title: The pipeline we build

scenes.caption: Two lists of 2,000 records: 4,000,000 possible pairs, of which 500 are true matches.
Candidate generation proposes a small set of pairs two ways. Anything it drops is lost for good, so we measure its recall of true pairs.
Only candidates are scored, then a threshold tuned on the labelled pairs decides which become links.

blocks.md:
**Candidates, way 1: character n-gram TF-IDF.** Each key becomes a sparse vector over its character 3-grams, weighted by TF-IDF (rare grams count more; the Inverted indexes and TF-IDF course explains the weighting), and two keys are compared by cosine similarity: the dot product of the two vectors divided by the product of their lengths, 1 when they point the same way. One sparse matrix product scores every pair that shares any gram; we keep the 5 best A records per B record. scikit-learn's `analyzer="char_wb"` makes n-grams only inside word boundaries, padding word edges with a space. Christen's survey of indexing methods uses the same TF-IDF and cosine on q-grams for canopy clustering.

**Candidates, way 2: MinHash LSH.** MinHash (the data pipeline lesson of the How LLMs are trained course covers it in depth) gives each padded 3-gram set a short signature whose agreement estimates Jaccard similarity; locality-sensitive hashing (LSH) cuts it into bands (the How LLMs are trained course calls them buckets) so that similar sets collide in some band.

blocks.code:
from recordlinkage.datasets import load_febrl4
from rapidfuzz import process, fuzz, utils
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from datasketch import MinHash, MinHashLSH

a, b = load_febrl4()
cols = ["given_name", "surname", "address_1", "suburb"]
key = lambda df, ids: [utils.default_process(" ".join(df.loc[i, cols].dropna())) for i in ids]
A = key(a, [f"rec-{i}-org" for i in range(2000)])
B = key(b, [f"rec-{i}-dup-0" for i in range(1500, 3500)])
truth = {(1500 + j, j) for j in range(500)}   # B[j] copies A[1500 + j]

# (a) char 3-gram TF-IDF, cosine by sparse product, top 5 per B record
vec = TfidfVectorizer(analyzer="char_wb", ngram_range=(3, 3))
XA = vec.fit_transform(A)
S = (vec.transform(B) @ XA.T).tocsr()
tfidf = {(int(i), j) for j in range(len(B))
         for i in S[j].indices[S[j].data.argsort()[::-1][:5]]}

# (b) MinHash LSH over padded 3-gram sets
def mh(s):
    m, s = MinHash(num_perm=128, seed=1), f"  {s} "
    for k in range(len(s) - 2):
        m.update(s[k:k + 3].encode())
    return m
lsh = MinHashLSH(threshold=0.5, num_perm=128)
for i, s in enumerate(A):
    lsh.insert(i, mh(s))
lshc = {(i, j) for j, s in enumerate(B) for i in lsh.query(mh(s))}

for name, c in [("tfidf", tfidf), ("lsh", lshc)]:
    print(name, len(c), "pairs, recall", len(c & truth) / 500)
print("b, r =", lsh.b, lsh.r)
M = process.cdist(B, A, scorer=fuzz.token_sort_ratio, workers=1)

# tfidf 10000 pairs, recall 1.0
# lsh 1448 pairs, recall 0.858
# b, r = 25 5
blocks.caption: Runnable on CPU (rapidfuzz, scikit-learn, datasketch, recordlinkage); output as run. The truth set works because B is ordered by original id.

blocks.md: datasketch's `MinHashLSH(threshold=0.5, num_perm=128)` chose b = 25 bands of r = 5 rows (its docs list the same choice). A stored set at Jaccard $s$ to the query shares at least one whole band, and so becomes a candidate, with probability:

blocks.caption: One band matches with probability s to the r (all r values must agree); 1 minus that is a miss, and all b bands must miss for the pair to be lost. With r = 5 and b = 25: P(0.5) = 0.548, P(0.7) = 0.990.

blocks.title: The LSH S-curve, with our measured retrieval

scenes.caption: r = 5, b = 25 (our index). Dots: share of our true pairs retrieved, by Jaccard bin of width 0.1 (20 to 88 pairs per bin). They follow the curve; few pairs per bin make the low bins noisy.
r = 9, b = 14: datasketch's choice for threshold 0.7. Longer bands are stricter, so pairs near 0.5 are almost never proposed.
r = 3, b = 37: the choice for threshold 0.3. More, shorter bands catch weak pairs, and many more non-matches with them.

blocks.title: Candidate generation: pairs kept, true pairs found, seconds

scenes.caption: Pairs to score: 4,000,000 for brute force, 10,000 from TF-IDF (5 per record), 1,448 from LSH. The candidate bars are barely visible: that is the point.
Recall of the 500 true pairs (percent). TF-IDF keeps all of them; LSH loses 14.2%, mostly pairs whose 3-gram Jaccard is below 0.5 (57 true pairs, of which it found 5).

Seconds in one run on one core of an Apple M5 Pro (timings vary with load; a rerun took 1.9 s for the first bar): all pairs with token_sort_ratio 1.06; TF-IDF candidates 0.19 plus 0.01 to score; LSH 0.79.

blocks.md:
At 2,000 by 2,000, brute force is still fast: `process.cdist(B, A, scorer=fuzz.token_sort_ratio, workers=1)` scored all 4,000,000 pairs in 1.06 s in our run (Jaro-Winkler: 0.31 s; timings vary with machine and load, and a rerun under load took 1.9 s). But it grows with the product of the list sizes. At that speed, 1 million by 1 million records is 250,000 times as many pairs, days of work on one core (an extrapolation from one measurement), while candidate generation only touches pairs that share grams or an LSH bucket. `cdist` and `extract` also take a `score_cutoff`, which lets RapidFuzz use the faster bounded algorithms from lesson 2.

Why did LSH miss pairs that TF-IDF kept? LSH applies an absolute bar (similar enough to collide), while top 5 is relative: the best five A records survive even when the best is weak, as for the reordered, damaged `fardwll alicia sunshine jeach`.

**Threshold selection.** For each B record take its best-scoring A record (fine here, where each record has at most one partner) and call it a link if the score reaches the threshold $t$. **Precision** is the share of predicted links that are true; **recall** is the share of the 500 true pairs that were linked. We compute both for every $t$ on the labelled pairs, for two scorers: `token_sort_ratio` and Jaro-Winkler (scaled to 0 to 100). The best partner is taken over all 4,000,000 scored pairs (the `cdist` matrix `M` in the code). Keeping only the TF-IDF top 5 gives the same precision and recall for `token_sort_ratio` from threshold 73 up, and fewer wrong links below it.

blocks.prompt: Will one threshold, say 85, work equally well for token_sort_ratio and Jaro-Winkler on these keys?
blocks.reveal: **No.** At 85, token_sort_ratio has precision 1.00 but recall only 0.67, while Jaro-Winkler has recall 0.84 but precision 0.61. Jaro-Winkler compresses everything near the top: on these 39-character keys the best-scoring A record, related or not, scores above 70 for almost every B record, so its useful range is around 88 to 90, while token_sort_ratio's is around 73 to 76.

blocks.title: Precision and recall vs threshold (percent)

scenes.caption: token_sort_ratio, precision: at 60 most predicted links point to the wrong record; from 75 up almost every link is correct.
token_sort_ratio, recall: it falls steadily as the bar rises; at 100 only copies with identical words survive (18.8%).
token_sort_ratio, F1 (the harmonic mean of precision and recall) peaks between 70 and 75; the fine sweep puts the best at 73 (F1 0.929).
Jaro-Winkler, precision: 23 to 32% up to 80, then 61% at 85 and a jump to 99.7% at 90. Same data, a very different curve.
Jaro-Winkler, recall: at its first high-precision threshold (90) it keeps 71.6% of true pairs, against 86% for token_sort_ratio at 75.

blocks.md:
Now pick a threshold for a stated goal. Say the business accepts at most 1 wrong link in 100 (precision at least 0.99): the lowest threshold that meets it is 76 for token_sort_ratio (precision 0.995, recall 0.852) and 89 for Jaro-Winkler (0.992 and 0.746). On these keys token_sort_ratio is the better scorer, because it forgives reordered words. A threshold copied from one scorer to another, or from someone else's data, means nothing.

Length matters too. Rerun on the name alone (given name and surname, 13 characters on average): at token_sort_ratio 90, names of up to 12 characters reach precision 0.747 and longer names 0.878, and no threshold reaches 0.99, because 47 records in B score 100 against a different person in A: namesakes, or names cut down to one field (`clarke` alone).

These numbers are for Febrl's synthetic corruption rates and a one-partner-per-record setup. Real data has its own typo rates, missing fields and namesakes, so tune on labelled pairs from your own data, and re-tune when the data or the key changes. With duplicates inside one list you also need clustering (entity-normalization).

Normalize, generate candidates with a method whose recall you have measured, score with a scorer that suits the key, then choose the threshold from a precision and recall sweep on labelled pairs, per scorer and, for short strings, per length.

blocks.question: An LSH index uses b = 25 bands of r = 5 rows. Roughly how likely is a pair with Jaccard similarity 0.5 to become a candidate?
options: About 0.55
Exactly 0.5, because MinHash estimates Jaccard
About 0.03
About 0.97
blocks.explain: One band matches with probability 0.5^5 = 0.031. All 25 bands miss with probability (1 - 0.031)^25 = 0.45, so P = 0.55. 0.03 is a single band; 0.97 would need many more bands.

blocks.question: Your linker reaches good precision on long names, but precision collapses on 3-character names such as `ali` or `lee`. What do you change?
options: Lower the global threshold so more short names match
Switch to token_set_ratio, which ignores extra words
Add more MinHash permutations
Make the threshold depend on length (exact or near-exact for very short strings, as Elasticsearch AUTO does) or require a second field to agree
blocks.explain: On short strings one edit is a large share of the string and unrelated names collide, so one global threshold is too loose for them. Length-dependent thresholds, or extra evidence from another field, restore precision. A lower threshold makes it worse, token_set_ratio adds subset matches, and permutations only change candidate generation.
